blocks.explain: The device can relay packets, but to decrypt it must complete the TLS handshake as bank.example, and that requires a trusted certificate and the matching private key. Without them the browser shows an error. The attack then depends on the user ignoring the warning.

blocks.md:
Real networks rarely connect a laptop straight to a server. Traffic passes through **intermediaries** that relay, wrap or filter it, and each one changes what the attacker and the defender can see.

RFC 9110 names the HTTP intermediaries precisely. A **proxy** (a stand-in acting for someone else) is chosen by the client, usually by configuration, and forwards its requests. A **gateway** (a different meaning from the default gateway router of lesson 5), better known as a **reverse proxy**, sits in front of servers and receives requests as if it were the server, then forwards them inbound. A **tunnel** blindly relays bytes between two connections without reading them, for example after an HTTP `CONNECT`.

blocks.title: Forward proxy and reverse proxy

scenes.caption: A company's forward proxy: employees' browsers send all web requests through it. The company can log, filter and, if devices trust its certificate, decrypt and inspect.
A website's reverse proxy: every visitor connects to it. It terminates TLS, filters attacks and spreads requests across application servers that are never exposed directly.

Consequence for logs: the application servers see the reverse proxy's address as the client. The real client address arrives in a header such as Forwarded (RFC 7239), which is only trustworthy if the proxy itself set it.

Consequence for attackers: a forward proxy is a single choke point that sees every request, and a reverse proxy is the only door into the application. Both are high-value targets and high-value log sources.

blocks.md:
A **VPN** (virtual private network: it behaves like a private link between you and a remote network, while actually running over shared public links) wraps your whole IP packets inside encrypted packets addressed to a VPN server. The server unwraps them and sends them on as if you were on its network. WireGuard, a modern VPN protocol, for example sends all its packets over UDP.

Companies use VPNs to give remote staff access to internal networks. Consumers use them to hide their traffic from the local network or ISP. In both cases the protection is between you and the VPN server only: beyond it, your traffic is as visible as before, and the VPN operator sees all of it.

blocks.title: Encapsulation inside a VPN tunnel

scenes.caption: The original packet: laptop 10.8.0.2 (its address inside the VPN) to an internal server 10.1.2.3, carrying HTTP.
The VPN encrypts the whole original packet, headers included.
Then it adds a new outer IP and UDP header: from the laptop's real address to the VPN server. This is what crosses the coffee shop Wi-Fi.
The local network sees only 'laptop talks UDP to VPN server', with sizes and timing. The VPN server removes the outer layer and forwards the original packet inside.

blocks.md:
A **firewall** is a device or program that allows or blocks traffic between networks according to rules. NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) describes the main kinds in its firewall guidelines, SP 800-41:

- **Packet filters** judge each packet alone by its addresses, ports and protocol.
- **Stateful inspection** also keeps a **state table** of connections (addresses, ports, connection state) and checks each packet against it, so a packet that claims to belong to an established connection that does not exist is dropped.
- **Application firewalls** understand application protocols, the "layer 7" devices of lesson 2.

NIST recommends **deny by default**: block everything not expressly permitted. Filtering incoming traffic is **ingress filtering** (a broader sense than the anti-spoofing BCP 38 filtering of lesson 4); filtering outgoing traffic is **egress filtering**, which can stop, for example, an infected machine from attacking others.

blocks.title: Evaluating packets against a small inbound ruleset

scenes.caption: Simplified model: rules are checked top to bottom and the first match decides. Rule 1 allows HTTPS from anywhere; rule 2 allows SSH only from the internal 10/8 network; rule 3 denies everything else.
A TCP packet from an external address to port 443 matches rule 1: allowed.
An external packet to SSH port 22: rule 1 fails (port), rule 2 fails (source not in 10/8), rule 3 matches: denied. The scanner from lesson 8 sees 'filtered'.
An internal admin at 10.0.5.9 connects to port 22: rule 2 matches, allowed.
Ordering bug: if 'any any any DENY' were moved above rule 1, nothing would ever be allowed; if a broad ALLOW sat on top, the deny would never be reached. Review rule order, not just rules.

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

RULES = [  # (protocol, source network, destination port, action); None means any
    ("tcp", "0.0.0.0/0", 443, "ALLOW"),
    ("tcp", "10.0.0.0/8", 22, "ALLOW"),
    (None,  "0.0.0.0/0", None, "DENY"),
]

def decide(proto, src, dport):
    for r_proto, r_src, r_port, action in RULES:          # top to bottom
        if (r_proto in (None, proto)
                and ip.ip_address(src) in ip.ip_network(r_src)
                and r_port in (None, dport)):
            return action                                  # first match wins
    return "DENY"                                          # nothing matched: deny by default

print(decide("tcp", "198.51.100.7", 443))   # ALLOW (rule 1)
print(decide("tcp", "198.51.100.7", 22))    # DENY  (rule 3)
print(decide("tcp", "10.0.5.9", 22))        # ALLOW (rule 2)
blocks.caption: The same simplified first-match ruleset as the figure, as code. Real firewalls add state tracking, interfaces, directions and logging.

blocks.md: A VPN is not anonymity and a firewall is not a security boundary for everything. The VPN provider sees what your ISP used to see, and a firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Each control answers one question; know which one.

blocks.question: A web application's logs show every request coming from 10.0.0.5, its own reverse proxy. An incident responder needs the attacker's real IP. Where should they look?
options: Nowhere, the real address is lost forever
In the application server's ARP cache
In the reverse proxy's own logs, or a forwarding header the proxy itself added
In the attacker's Set-Cookie header
blocks.explain: The reverse proxy accepted the original connection, so its logs hold the client address, and it can pass that on in a header such as Forwarded. A forwarding header sent by the client itself proves nothing, since clients can write any header they like.

blocks.question: Using the ruleset above, an external host sends a TCP packet to port 3389. What happens, and which recommendation does that reflect?
options: Denied by rule 3, reflecting NIST's deny-by-default advice
Allowed by rule 1, because it is TCP
Allowed by rule 2, because 3389 is a user port
Dropped by NAT, not by the firewall
blocks.explain: Rules 1 and 2 require ports 443 and 22, so neither matches; the final rule denies. Because the ruleset ends in a catch-all deny, a service someone forgets to list stays blocked rather than exposed.

lessons.title: Reading a packet capture like a defender

blocks.md:
A **packet capture** records copies of the packets that pass a point in the network, usually into a **pcap** file (packet capture, the format of the libpcap library). Two tools dominate. **tcpdump** is a command-line program that captures and prints packets, one line each. **Wireshark** (formerly called Ethereal, per its FAQ) is a graphical analyzer: a packet list, a pane that decodes every header field of the selected packet layer by layer, and the raw bytes. Both read the same files.

Where you capture decides what you see. As lesson 3 showed, a switch sends your port only your own traffic plus broadcasts. To watch other machines, defenders capture on the hosts themselves, on a gateway, or on a switch **mirror port** configured to copy traffic to a sensor.

Two kinds of filter, easy to confuse:

- A **capture filter** decides which packets are recorded at all. It uses the [pcap-filter](https://www.tcpdump.org/manpages/pcap-filter.7.html) language of the libpcap library (often called BPF syntax, because libpcap compiles it into programs for BPF, the Berkeley Packet Filter, the packet-filtering engine inside the operating system kernel): `tcp port 443`, `host 192.168.1.66`, `arp or udp port 53`.
- A **display filter** is Wireshark's language for hiding and showing packets already captured, using named fields: `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0`, `dns.qry.name contains "example"`, `http.request.method == "POST"`, `arp.duplicate-address-detected`, `tcp.analysis.retransmission`.

blocks.code:
# Capture DNS and HTTPS on your own lab interface into a file (needs admin rights)
sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 -w lab.pcap 'udp port 53 or tcp port 443'

# Read it back later, showing only connection attempts (SYN without ACK)
tcpdump -n -r lab.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn'

# -n  no name lookups (faster, and does not send DNS queries that tip anyone off)
# -w  write raw packets to a file;  -r  read packets from a file
blocks.caption: tcpdump basics. Open the same lab.pcap in Wireshark to explore it with display filters.

blocks.title: Reading an illustrative capture line by line

scenes.caption: Lines 1 and 2: the laptop asks who has the gateway's IP and gets the router's MAC (ending 53:fe). Normal start of any conversation.
Lines 3 and 4: a DNS query with ID 4660 ('+' means recursion desired) for an A record; the answer has 1 answer record, 198.51.100.10. Numbers in brackets are DNS message lengths.
Lines 5 to 7: the handshake to port 443. In tcpdump flags, S is SYN, . is ACK, P is PSH, R is RST, F is FIN. It prints the first sequence numbers in full, then relative ones (ack 1).
Line 8: 517 bytes with PSH and ACK right after the handshake on port 443: almost certainly a TLS ClientHello. From here on, content is encrypted.
Lines 9 to 11: 192.168.1.66 sends SYN to port 22, gets SYN-ACK, and answers with RST instead of completing. That is a half-open SYN scan finding an open port.
Lines 12 to 14: same source, same source port, next ports 23 and 25. Port 23 answers RST (closed), 25 is silent (filtered). One host walking through ports: a scan.
Line 15: a new ARP reply says 192.168.1.1 is now at ..53:66, not the router's ..53:fe. One IP, two MACs within seconds: likely ARP spoofing, right after a scan. Escalate.

blocks.md:
**What defenders look for in captures and flow data:**

1. **Scanning:** one source, many destination ports or hosts, many SYNs with RST or no reply.
2. **Layer 2 trickery:** one IP claimed by two MACs, unexpected DHCP servers.
3. **DNS oddities:** bursts of random subdomains of one domain, very long names (possible DNS tunnelling: data smuggled out inside query names), many failed lookups (the 'name error' response code, usually called NXDOMAIN), lookups of freshly registered names.
4. **Cleartext secrets:** Telnet, FTP (File Transfer Protocol) or HTTP logins and session cookies crossing the wire unencrypted.
5. **Beaconing:** a host contacting the same external address at regular intervals, a common sign of malware checking in with its controller.
6. **Volume anomalies:** traffic ratios that flip, as GitHub saw in 2018.

Captures contain other people's data: passwords, messages, cookies. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor, keep the files protected, and delete them when done. Intercepting others' traffic without authorisation is illegal in most countries (the security basics course covers the law).

**Practice legally.** Download real traces from the [Wireshark sample captures](https://wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures) page and find the handshakes, DNS lookups and ARP exchanges from this course. Capture your own traffic at home while browsing a few sites. Then try forensics and network challenges on [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (formerly picoCTF, Carnegie Mellon University), the beginner wargames on [OverTheWire](https://overthewire.org/wargames/), the free rooms on [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/), and the free defensive investigations on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/).

blocks.question: In Wireshark you want only packets where a host tries to open a TCP connection. Which display filter is right?
options: tcp port 80
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0
tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0
tcp.flags.reset == 1
blocks.explain: A connection attempt is the first handshake segment: SYN set, ACK not set. `tcp port 80` and the `tcp[tcpflags]` expression are capture filter (pcap-filter) syntax, not display filter syntax, and the `tcp[tcpflags]` one would also match SYN-ACKs. Resets are a different event.

blocks.question: A capture shows a laptop resolving a random-looking 40-character subdomain of the same unknown domain every 60 seconds, each followed by a small HTTPS connection to the same IP. What is the best reading?
options: Normal software update checks, nothing to see
An ARP spoofing attack in progress
A TCP SYN flood against the laptop
Possible malware beaconing to a controller, worth isolating the host and investigating
